subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER FOLLOWING OBSERVATION OF SEAL HUNT
STATEMENT BY MINISTER FOLLOWING OBSERVATION OF SEAL HUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement on the seal hunt, for two reasons: One is to announce that the hunt itself is to be postponed for the remainder of this week because of exceptional conditions on the ice; and the other is to allay certain fears which have been expressed as to the manner in which in recent days the hunt has been carried out in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Having spent some time on the ice over the week end and having talked to a number of
veterinarians from western Europe, the United States and Canada, I am of the opinion that the seal hunt is being supervised in an effective manner. The Fisheries Department's regulations are being enforced and the suffering of the young seals is being kept to a minimum.
For most of us who were out on the ice over the weekend, the hunt itself was a gruesome sight. The killing process was undoubtedly effective. It was effective because it was carried out with dispatch and by men who had killed young seals before. But I could not help asking myself whether the hunt in the Gulf of St. Lawrence was really necessary in the first place.
Some 6,000 Canadians depend, for at least part of their livelihood, on the seal hunt. However, they are not always the same people since the seals follow the ice and the ice may be west of Les lies de la Madeleine one year and north of Prince Edward Island the next.
One thing is predictable, however: It is the impressive sight of the great seal herd itself. If we could convert this unique happening into an annual tourist attraction it could also contribute materially to the economy of the Atlantic region. I think we must therefore explore the possibility of the Gulf of St. Lawrence being declared a sanctuary for seals, with the hunt itself being limited to international waters in the north Atlantic off Labrador and Newfoundland.
Ice conditions this year are exceptional. The ice itself is poor in quality and limited in area. Also the use of helicopters has tended to prevent the mother seals from pupping on the ice. There is a danger of many young seals being lost under these conditions, and I have therefore declared a moratorium on the hunt beginning at 6 p.m. tonight and continuing through until 6 a.m. Friday morning.
The situation south of Prince Edward Island, where the main seal herds are located, is of course being kept under review and other protective measures will be announced as required.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER FOLLOWING OBSERVATION OF SEAL HUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know all members on this side of the house listened with interest to the statement made today by the Minister of Fisheries

March 10, 1969
Questions
(Mr. Davis) with regard to the seal hunt. I ana sure all of us welcome his announcement that his personal investigation of this hunt showed there was no cruelty involved. I find it rather difficult however to picture a seal hunt as a tourist attraction, in view of the difficulties involved in getting to the area concerned. I doubt that this could ever become a possibility.
The minister has announced that the seal hunt is to be postponed for the remainder of this week because of exceptional conditions on the ice. I hope the number of days on which the hunt is restricted will be made available to the hunters by an extension of the hunting season. I also note the minister's comments regarding the hunt and the fact that he found it gruesome. Quite frankly, killing, whether it be in a vast outdoor abattoir like the sealhunt or whether it is conducted in a regular abattoir, is not a very pleasant sight. However the method used by the sealers is humane. As the minister stated, he found this to be the case. It is humane in that it stuns the seal.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Since this industry makes an important contribution to the livelihood of some 6,000 people in the Atlantic provinces we on this side of the house hope that the industry will be maintained. The minister has suggested exploring the possibility of declaring the Gulf of St. Lawrence a sanctuary for seals, with the hunt being limited to international waters in the North Atlantic off Labrador and Newfoundland. This may have some merit from a conservation angle. I believe any move along this line should be thoroughly discussed with other countries concerned, in order that we do not find ourselves taking unilateral action to conserve our seal herds while other nations take an unlimited kill.
I welcome some of the minister's statements and I hope he will take my suggestions seriously and discuss them at the next international conference on the law of the sea, which he has indicated from time to time may soon be held.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER FOLLOWING OBSERVATION OF SEAL HUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I attended the hunt on Friday and Saturday last with the minister and I found there were almost more newspaper reporters and inspectors than there were fishermen. I too felt that the extra aircraft activity and the people attending disturbed the seals somewhat.

As far as cruelty is concerned in respect of these animals, I do not believe there was any cruelty or inhumane treatment, if you consider the method in this case. I think it was done as mercifully as could be done and I would be critical of those who have reported otherwise.
I think this industry is important as a means of increasing income for the people in this area, and certainly they are people who could use an increase in income.
Finally I would suggest that any effort to conserve seal herds should be done by agreement with other countries. I do not think it is right, proper or fitting that Canada should attempt to look after an international resource as a result of which our people would suffer reductions to income, if other nations are not willing to go along in this respect.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER FOLLOWING OBSERVATION OF SEAL HUNT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once again', we learn that the laws of nature delay the seal hunt. We have even been told that over the weekend more than 2,000 young seals drowned since they cannot swim until they are 10 days old. Let us hope that next season the seal hunt will not enable only some American millionaires to make money, but on the contrary will enable some Canadians to earn a living for that period in that area of Canada.

My understanding is that the first item of business called for today is the government reorganization bill, which by special order is being considered in committee of the whole. When debate adjourned on this item of business on February 28, clause 7 of the bill was under consideration. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we left the subject of the bill on February 28 we were dealing with the changes that are to take place in the Post Office Department and other departments of government in order to form the new Department of Communications. I realize there are some hon. members who want to speak on a matter of considerable urgency with which we dealt during the course of the question period, but I want this afternoon to deal with two or three points not related particularly to postal services but which came to my mind and are important so far as communications are concerned.
The first point I want to deal with particularly is the title of the new department. It is to be known as the Department of Communications, although in the bill it is stated that the minister is also to be known as the Postmaster General. I presume that he is to be known as the Postmaster General rather in the way that the Minister of Finance is also known as the Receiver General, a title which is used officially or for purposes of departmental administration, and is in the act but is not really used publicly in the minister's title.
I wish to refer to a debate which took place in the house during the last parliament in connection with the establishment of the title of Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Hon. members will remember that at that time it was first thought that the minister's title should be Minister of Manpower and that the word "Immigration" should be dropped. I think hon. members opposite raised the point that the word "Immigration" is so firmly fixed in the public mind, so well
Government Organization understood, indeed, that it should be associated with the title of the minister. This was agreed, an amendment was made in the house and the title of the minister was finally decided upon as being Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
The suggestion I make this afternoon is simply that we should not abolish the words "postal services" and the title "Postmaster General" but should make an attempt to retain a title so well known throughout Canada and the world in mail or postal services. My suggestion is that the title should not be abridged to that of Minister of Communications, or Department of Communications but that the department should be known as the Department of Communications and Postal Services.
When someone in the country wants to complain about the mail service the department he requires should be listed clearly in the telephone directory. He should not be put off his stride by hunting through the telephone book and not finding old and familiar words. Therefore I plead for the retention in the title of the words "Postal Services", and for the department to be called the Department of Communications and Postal Services.

So there it is. He has 48,000 employees and 8,000 branches in the Post Office Department, and he wants to eliminate the words "Postal Services" or "Post Office" from the title of the department.
I want to deal more specifically this afternoon with a different topic. I refer to the subject of communications in its new role as the minister explained it and apart from the Post Office. In his speech the minister said:
Combined and rationalized under a single minister are all of the government's activities in the field of communications, that is both communications in its modern, electronic sense, and communications in its traditional sense of the Post Office.
A little later he said:
-the object of this legislation is to make a single minister responsible for all government activities in the field of communications.
Then he said:
-the Minister of Communications is responsible for two departments, each headed by a deputy minister, and also for a number of government agencies. The departments are, of course, the Department of Communications itself and the Post Office. The agencies which will now report to parliament through the Minister of Communications are the C.O.T.C., the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation; the Canadian Transport Commission, but specifically only that segment of the C.T.C. concerned with the regulation of telecommunication rates, and, once it is established by legislation, the domestic satellite corporation.
These are functions now carried on by the air services division of the Department of Transport and by its telecommunications and electronics branch. I want to refer you, Mr. Chairman, to a part of the description of that branch as set out in "Organization of the Government of Canada", the official volume describing the functions of departments and branches of the government. It says:
The functions of the telecommunications and electronics branch include: the ... use of radio for safety of life in the air and on the seas; construction, maintenance and operation of aeronautical, marine and meteorological radio-communication stations and of radio and electronic aids to navigation associated with airports and domestic and international airways, and with marine navigation along the sea coasts of Canada and on the Great Lakes-
The reason I have given these quotations and this background in some detail is in order to ask some questions to which clear answers should be given before we give final approval to the bill. Does the bill mean that the communication functions of airports and air and marine navigation are now to come under the new ministry? Are there to be two

The operative words in the amendments are the following:

To me this simply means that the Postmaster General as we know him today is not only to be in the D.O.T. tower at the airport but that he has climbed aboard every aircraft in the land and also every ship. I am not prepared at this time to condemn this arrangement, but I want to know if this is so. If it is so, why is it better, safer, simpler and cheaper than it was under the air services division and the former ministry?
The Department of Transport was put together in 1936 by the late C. D. Howe when he amalgamated the old department of railways and canals, the department of marine, and the civil aviation branch of the Department of National Defence. It became such a large empire that every prime minister and minister since that time has thought of splitting it up. On September 17, 1964, Mr. Balcer, a former minister of transport, said the following in the House of Commons:
-I believe that it would make sense to take the management of the civil aviation division away from the Department of Transport.
March 10, 1969

That is found at page 8120 of Hansard of September 17, 1964. Mr. Glassco suggested the idea in volume 5 of his report when he said at page 44:
-would the public interest be better served by the creation of a separate ministry to give more single-minded attention to the problems of civil aviation, or by maintaining the present organization as a more suitable context within which to attack the broader problems of transportation policy?
Of all the suggestions for carving up the Department of Transport, the one that consistently has made the most sense to us over' the years has been the establishment of a ministry for air. Canada has a long and outstanding history in air transportation. Most modem nations have long since established separate air ministries. Communication is such an integral part of the operation of air services that one would have thought it more logical to establish an air ministry and let it be the agency for communication services which are now to be lumped with the Post Office.
Let me turn again to Mr. Glassco for an opinion. In volume 2 of his report, page 251, he says this in discussing telecommunications:
-there is no case for unified management of government telecommunications. But there is need for central policy and authority to ensure that a cohesive and economic pattern will evolve.
Telecommunications must be recognized to be, first and foremost, a supporting service essential to the conduct of operations. Consequently, the individual departments and agencies, as the active operating organizations of government, must bear the primary responsibility for determining what telecommunications are necessary to the success of their programs, and for ensuring the effectiveness of those services. In these respects, the management of telecommunications differs in no way from that of other supporting services.
The question then arises: To what extent is the new department to be simply a policymaking department, and to what extent is it to take over operating functions?
In summary, my main questions to the minister as he takes up his new duties are these: First, are we emasculating the air services division in such a way that it can no longer hope to be an effective single component capable of one day becoming a ministry for air? I think that is a very important problem for members to consider today in this chamber as we discuss this bill. Second, are we centralizing the operation of communications, taking it away from departments as a supporting service, and moving in the opposite direction to the one recommended by Mr. Glassco? If so, what have we found in the interval since the Glassco report that has

Government Organization brought about the decision to head off in a direction counter to that taken by him in his recommendations? Are we putting two ministers in charge of air control where now there is one minister and one team?
This is a matter that deserves thoughtful consideration by the house for it has to do with air navigation, sea navigation and the safety of people travelling by air and on sea. Have we made the right decision in giving telecommunications to a department which has heretofore been unassociated with it, or should it have been left with air services where there are operators as well as inspectors and licensers with many years of experience in the Department of Transport, the principal user of communications in the country?
I think these are pertinent questions. I am not a technician in the field, I am not highly skilled in it, and I am not competent to answer these questions. But they are certainly questions which come to my mind when I read the bill and ones to which I think the minister should address himself when he tells us how the decisions were reached in regard to the organization of the new Department of Communications. I will listen to him with great interest when the opportunity comes for him to explain these points.

Now it is proposed to establish another monster over which parliament will have no control. I think of a number of these Crown corporations which are costing the taxpayers many millions of dollars each year and over which parliament has no effective control whatsoever. I do not want to see the minister lose control of the Post Office. I think that over the years Canada can be proud of its postal services; some fine personnel have served in the department. Surely the minister could get together three or four men from the postal service and have them cross the nation to find out why the public is not better served. He told us the mail must be delivered. Well, the mail is not being delivered. This may be due in part to the ending of Saturday deliveries, but I do not know why it should take from Wednesday to the following Tuesday for a letter posted in Toronto to be delivered in Ottawa. I believe the minister should take a team from the Post Office and have a thorough investigation made. I do not wish to appear, by being silent, to endorse what is going on.
My hon. friend from Hillsborough complimented the Postmaster General on some of his new ideas. But the minister has aggravated the present situation by threatening postal workers with prosecution if they do not behave. I, personally, do not believe that the old innstrument of strikes ought to be used by people in the public service of Canada. I do not think it works out very well. This is my own view; I have not discussed it with my party. Surely in this modem age, given the capabilities and the knowledge of management and labour, these problems could be worked out without disrupting essential services such as the railroads and the mail. Remember, though, it was a Liberal government which gave those engaged ini the public service the right to strike. It was they who brought in- the necessary act of parliament to this effect, and responsibility for so doing rests on their shoulders.

DEBATES	March 10, 1969
Again, instead of acting in a logical way by appointing someone to arbitrate the issue now in dispute, the Postmaster General says he intends to prosecute those concerned. Mr. Chairman, he cannot make anyone in Canada believe he intends to prosecute all the mailmen, because there are not enough jails to hold them all.
We on this side of the house opposed certain moves to increase postal rates. We said the increase would kill off the weekly newspapers, the farm papers and the periodicals. As we predicted, they are gradually going broke. Even Maclean's has been reduced in size: it is now a little magazine. Farm papers have gone broke, Weekly newspapers have gone broke. At the same time this government, for some reason, still subsidizes Time magazine and Reader's Digest to the extent of about $1,500,000 each year. Canadian papers do not enjoy this advantage. I do not know whether the government has such a monopoly on good news in Time that they hate to destroy it. Perhaps they ought to take the news across the nations using Time magazine, but it seems to me they are discriminating against Canadian periodicals.
I intend now to make a serious charge against the Post Office Department, and I am not imputing any blame to the minister in this regard. While he is making a check on the working of the Post Office I think he should look into it. Arrangements exist under which, on payment of so much per pound, mail is delivered to householders throughout a city. During election campaigns candidates of all parties use this method of getting their literature into homes of constituents. It is also widely used by business houses. In Calgary North there are 26,436 houses, 2,874 apartments and 1,191 businesses. I believe it costs from $400 to $600 to have mail delivered to householders in Calgary. What happened? Bundles of advertising put out by various department stores in Calgary as well as election pamphlets of mine were found out in a ditch two or three miles north of Calgary in- a place called Airdrie. The Post Office was contacted immediately. Investigators went there and took photographs. They found the undelivered mail there in bundles. Since then f have written frequently to the department asking for an explanation. Apart from anything else, I feel that if mail is not delivered the least the department can do is to refund the money which has been paid. But nothing has been done in this regard. The minister talks about reorganization. He should make arrangements to investigate the causes of poor mail service. At present, it is a disgrace. I feel sorry for the hon. gentleman. No doubt he inherited part of the problem, but it appears to be getting worse. Has he failed to arouse any initiative among the officials with whom he comes into contact? A question was asked by my right hon. friend from Prince Albert with reference to the time taken for a letter to be delivered from Calgary. What did the minister say in his reply? It is the quality of the service that should concern him. Why did he not begin an inquiry immediately to see whether he could not get some service back into the Post Office, especially at a time of increased rates?
This afternoon parliament is being asked to give birth to another monster. Once a Crown corporation has been created, I know what the minister will say in reply to questions and

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word of sympathy for the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra respecting the point he raised to the effect that the words "Post Office Department" should not disappear from telephone directories and other such places. However, I submit, having read the various clauses in the bill, that this is not likely to happen. The department over which the present minister
March 10, 1969

Government Organization will preside will be known mainly as the Department of Communications and the minister will be addressed as the Minister of Communications. However, according to my reading of clause 12 of the bill there is to be continued a department in the government of Canada which will be called the Post Office Department and the presiding minister is to be the Postmaster General.
Clause 12 also makes it clear that the Minister of Communications will be the Postmaster General. In other words, whoever heads up this phase of governmental activity will wear two hats. I suspect that as far as the general public is concerned the main interest for a long time will be in the Post Office Department, and the Post Office Department will certainly be listed in the telephone directory and be there for people to consult and deal with.
I rise this afternoon mainly to make an earnest plea to the minister to establish proper employer-employee relations in the Post Office Department, and to get at this with speed.
We have had a good deal to say during the course of this session about changes with respect to the Post Office Department that we do not like. We do not like the higher charges and the reduced service. We do not like the five-day delivery schedule. We do not like all of the things that have been complained about under these various headings. I think that the minister is being callous in his failure to be concerned about non-profit publications and so on. But I submit that the element that can do the most damage to the service of the Post Office Department is the development of a tradition of bad employer-employee relations.
I know that the minister has been running around to the various post offices in Canada, visiting the workers, eating lunches in their cafeterias and so on, and that he prides himself on being a person who is interested in good employer-employee relations. But, with respect, I would submit to him that on the issue that is causing trouble in many cities in Canada today he is completely off base.
In his reply to a question or two on orders of the day this afternoon, the minister said that he saw no relationship between this matter and the Freedman report. I submit that there is a very close relationship between the recommendations of the Freedman report and what some of us are asking in connection with the present situation. As a matter of fact, I submit that there is close proximity between
tMr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).]

the problem that initiated the Freedman inquiry and the problem here.
The Freedman report came about because of run-throughs that were established by the Canadian National Railways which the employees of that company felt were unfair. The mess the Post Office is in today is the result of the walk-throughs that the Post Office Department has implemented and that it requires its workers to carry out. The minister might quarrel with that expression, but I am referring to the new arrangement under which there is only one sortation of mail per day by the letter carriers, following which they go out on their walks and are not permitted to return to their post offices at noon. So I submit that in effect it is a walkthrough that has been instituted.
The Postmaster General was quite correct in his statement on orders of the day this afternoon that the Freedman report recognizes that management has certain rights and that there are certain things that management can change. But the Freedman report also says that where there are essential or extensive changes in work patterns, changes that are made after a collective agreement has been signed with the employees should be subject to negotiation before they are put into effect. I readily recognize that there can be an argument over whether a certain change is minor or extensive, but surely the annoyance that has been felt by letter carriers across Canada over the change that has been put into effect is because, at least in their minds, they feel this is not a minor change but is in fact extensive change in their work pattern.
I submit that if the government has any respect at all for the Freedman report, this is a matter that ought to have been negotiated before the change was put into effect. But what have the Postmaster General and the Post Office Department done about the matter? The change has been put into effect without negotiation. A set of rules has been laid down that the workers must carry out. When the workers start to resist because they think these rules are grossly unfair and are really a violation of their contract, the Postmaster General takes the case to the Public Service Staff Relations Board to apply for permission to prosecute. It is now reported to us that these men may individually be subject to fines of $100 each for each day they are out, and that the unions themselves may be subject to fines of $500 a day. When the situation gets even worse and the response to these threats is for even more men to walk out and
March 10, 1969

refuse to deliver mail under duress, under these conditions, the minister says that it has now been agreed to skip two or three stages of the grievance procedure and have the issue adjudicated by a third party.
I suggest to the Postmaster General that this is precisely the wrong way to go about this matter. In the first place, you should not impose a change by arbitrary fiat, hand out threats, and then while insisting that the rules still be carried out have a so-called third party adjudication. I submit that if this matter is to be dealt with satisfactorily in terms of achieving good employer-employee relations, the Post Office Department ought right away to suspend these walk-throughs until there has been a chance for the employer and the employees to negotiate them, determine whether they are an acceptable pattern of work, whether they fit in with the machinery of the Post Office and whether they form lines of work that are reasonable for the men to carry out.
* (4:00 p.m.)
There is a good deal to be said for the challenge postal workers have held out to the Postmaster General in which they asked him to report for work at some specified place and go through the kind of day that has been proposed for them. Arbitrary rules are imposed on our workers. The department says that its actions will save the country $3 million and therefore the workers ought to like it. The net result is a worsening in employer-employee relations. Nothing can do more damage to our postal service than this kind of situation.
Even if the Postmaster General alleges that progress has been made in straightening out some situations in the postal service since he took over the department, he must admit that the present situation is not good and that the machinery within the department is moving slowly. Even though the department may be moving slowly, it is not moving in the right direction. The five-day delivery schedule is proving to be a failure, and service to the public is becoming worse. Various factors, such as higher costs and other changes the Postmaster General and his officials have tried to make, have contributed to that situation. But the basic, crucial factor we ought to consider is the matter of employer-employee relations.
In my view, the Postmaster General is going about his business in this area in the wrong way. Only this afternoon could he tell
Government Organization us about the third party adjudication which might take place. We do not know the terms and conditions under which this adjudication will be put into effect. I submit that for the government to keep to its walk-through rules while the matter is being adjudicated is not conducive to producing a good rapport between employer and employees in this important and vital service. Before the situation gets worse, I ask the Postmaster General to apply common sense to the matter of achieving good employer-employee relations in his department. The time to do this is now.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking on the bill to reorganize the government and among other things, set up a new communications department I must say that while we are providing for a great deal of new communication from the sky we are seriously neglecting the communications that may be delivered through small, rural post offices in the many small communities scattered across the country. The Post Office Department has set about with a vengeance to close many small, rural post offices and, in effect, to reduce service to rural people. I do not say that all rural post offices ought to be left open indefinitely. From time to time many of them will have to be closed. As a result of reorganization within the department many rural post offices will close. On the other hand, the closing of some of these post offices will bring little saving to the department. In such cases there will be reduced service to the patrons of the post office and, consequently, a reduction in service to the community as a whole.
I do not feel that the method of closing our rural post offices is fair. A decision to close a post office is taken only after there has been an investigation of the amount of stamps and money orders sold by that post office. The fact is that the stamps sold are used on only a small portion of the mail that passes through the post office. After all, the patrons of small post offices receive much more mail than they send and it seems only fair that the revenue from a portion of the mail received should be credited to that post office. Indeed, if the small rural post office is fortunate enough to be patronized by a business it has justification for remaining open notwithstanding the fact that the business in question could well use the post office of a larger centre.
Many patrons are being provided with a rural route service which costs between $18 and $20 for each patron. As labour costs rise, so will the cost of this service. Generally, once a post office has been established in an area,
March 10, 1969

Government Organization patrons prefer its services to those supplied under the rural route system. The Postmaster General ought to take a second look at revenue considerations under which the department decides whether a post office shall be closed. Also, rural post offices should be closed more gradually. A definite formula for their closing ought to be established and the postmasters and people of the communities concerned ought to be given ample warning that this vital service is to be closed down.
So far officials of the department do not seem to have visited local post offices serving reduced numbers of patrons. There has been no suggestion to postmasters concerned that they should carry on in a lower category, so to speak, so that the remuneration received by the post office will be more in line with the service it provides.
Having made these comments, I suggest that drastic and sudden reorganizations at the local level have caused serious unrest. Many rural people feel the post office has written them off because they use it too little. After all, it is little use having the Post Office Department make substantial savings at the cost of not giving our people service. It also seems that the Post Office is making it difficult for rural people to receive magazines and farm periodicals. The increases in postage rates for these publications will cause severe hardships. Increases ranging between seven cents and twenty cents are the order of the day and, if continued, will dislocate the dissemination of the written word throughout these communities. True, increased postage rates for publications were overdue. Nevertheless, the department's sudden attempt to wipe out its deficit in this field can result only in serious dislocation to the detriment of the farming community.
Fewer periodicals will be published. The reduced volume of mail may increase the department's deficit beyond what has been projected. Mailing rates which have been severely and extensively increased will bring about drastic and sudden readjustments in all our industries. The government has relied on farm newspapers to disseminate much information to the farming community. Although it may be said that the government departments concerned should pay to have information disseminated to the farming community, such a step will take time. The net result of the postage increases may be a catastrophic decrease in the circulation of the printed word. We may lose more than we gain.
[Mr. Kitchie.i
The attitude of the Post Office to its workers leaves much to be desired. The Postmaster General's attitude, that he will prosecute the workers and unions, seems severe and inflexible. The working conditions of letter carriers have been drastically altered and more time is needed to iron out the problems of the five-day week.
Often the Post Office Department forgets that people are human, with personal needs that must be met. It seems that the department ought to adopt a more rational approach to the question of straight-through delivery. The department appears to be belligerent toward the workers and has not been willing to accept suggestions from the workers as to how these problems ought to be worked out. Straight-through delivery is a great change from what the carrier has been used to, and it will take the carrier time to become adjusted to this change. In many cases where washrooms facilities are not readily available the change may be impossible to effect. The unions' position is that straight-through delivery is a change in the terms of the labour contract. I think this is a reasonable attitude and one that calls for adjudication by third parties. I ask the minister to accept third-party adjudication as the best solution to the problem.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The minister's attitude seems to be very stiffnecked and uncompromising. It is the same attitude that he has displayed with reference to rural post offices and periodicals. Complete reorganization of the Post Office Department will take time. The minister should know that Rome was not built in a day. A more conciliatory and sympathetic attitude to the problems of the workers would stand the minister in good stead. I urge him to re-examine his whole approach to the problems of the Post Office Department.
The people of Canada would not fault the minister in any way if he took more time to make his changes in the postal services, many of which are good and necessary, but I point out that severe changes can cause dislocation even when they are right and proper. I would ask the minister to proceed more slowly. I believe the result would be much better. The people of Canada will not thank the minister for suddenly making the Post Office pay if the service they get is poor and inadequate. Both goals can be achieved gradually if the minister is reasonable in his approach to the problem.
March 10. 1969

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity to make use of the suggestion Mr. Speaker made to us earlier today, when we asked for adjournment of the house to debate the important issue of the threatened postal strike, that we would have an opportunity when this bill came before us. We are facing a very serious situation. We might be in for another postal strike. I sincerely hope the minister is dealing with the matter in the serious way that it requires.
I am surprised the Postmaster General did not realize what lay before him in the reorganization of the Post Office Department. I and many other members of the house do not understand why he did not sit down with the postal officials and say: Gentlemen, we are going to change the sorting arrangements. The postmen will sort all their mail in the morning and then deliver the whole day's mail. They will no longer return to the post office after lunch as they did previously and sort the afternoon mail. He should have asked his legal authorities this question: Is this in violation of the existing contract? Had he done so we would not be in the serious situation of being threatened with another postal strike.
The department's public relations have been poor. If the Postmaster General had given his full attention to these proposed changes rather than going about the country talking about NATO, about satellites and about new communications systems it would have been better, at least until his reorganization was working smoothly.
The people of Canada have been asked to pay higher postage rates. For this they expect better service. But instead they are getting worse service. Canada is the first country I know of that has endeavoured to deliver a week's mail in five days. The minister has tried to bulldoze this change through without the proper public relations and without the proper prior thought and study. Many warnings were given to the minister, but instead of allowing the issue to cool off he heats up the situation by making public threats to the staff. I hope he realizes how serious the situation is.
I am receiving many complaints about poor postal service, particularly from persons in the retail trade and more particularly from storekeepers in areas where stores are closed on Mondays. If a storekeeper gets a letter on Friday morning he cannot reply to it until the following Tuesday.
Government Organization
As an example I cite a jeweller who sends watches away to be repaired. If he does not get a watch back by mail on Friday he will have to wait until the following Tuesday. I maintain that the retail sections of our communities are entitled to six-day service. In many cases their very livelihood depends on the mail. Now they are told to rent postal boxes in the local post offices in order to get six-day service. If this continues many post offices will not be large enough to hold all the rented boxes. I beg the minister to give consideration to the retail outlets and business offices and provide them with better service.
I have also received many complaints about counter service in post offices. By counter service I mean the service given at the main counter on the main floor of a post office where there is the stamp wicket, the registration wicket, the C.O.D. parcels wicket, and all the rest down the line. What happens at this counter now on Saturdays? There are two workers in our post office on Saturday mornings and they have been given instructions not to do any business. They are there to hand out registered letters and parcels on receipt of cards left by the local postman on his rounds. But they cannot sell a stamp, they cannot weigh a letter or do other business of any kind. I say to the Postmaster General, either do business on the main floor with complete counter service, or close the place up. Let there be no half measure about it. If a post office is open let it do business at all wickets and not just one or two.
There is no reason in the world that we should not be getting next day delivery across the country. We get next day delivery from Europe and many other countries. But it takes two days, three days and sometimes four days for letters posted in Toronto to reach their destinations at London, Guelph and other places no more than 80 miles away. As I said previously when speaking on the estimates of the Post Office Department, we had better mail delivery in the days of the stage coach than we have today. There is something radically wrong, and I take this opportunity of bringing it to the minister's attention once again.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I shall not take any more of the time of the house. I regret that the Postmaster General did not sit down with these men and with the heads of his department to see whether there was any possibility that the existing contract may have been violated. If this had been
6412	COMMONS DEBATES	March 10. 1969
Government Organization done thoroughly I do not think the Post Office would be involved in the mumbo-jumbo it seems to be involved in today. With these few words I shall sit down in the hope that the Postmaster General will be successful in smoothing out the problems with his staff so that better public relations will exist in the future. Then we'll have better service.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in 1912 Sir Richard Cartwright said that no man and no party can be safely entrusted with uncontrolled power. I would hope that this is is not the reason we have received the answers we have received in the last while whenever a question has been asked concerning postal service. Some of the questions which were asked today were very sincere and sincere answers should have been given. Unfortunately one cannot help but be disappointed that the Postmaster General would use threatening language when dealing with a labour dispute and tell civil servants how they must bargain. Surely the federal government should lead the way in respect of collective bargaining in this country. I belieVe the Freedman report set the stage for this. I am very disappointed that the minister would stand up and suggest he is not prepared to allow freedom of collective bargaining to these people as it is recognized by the public service.
I am completely in favour of the bill passed by this house which allowed public servants to strike. I believe this is a human right of every individual and I believe they should be given this prerogative. With regard to changes in the working conditions of any employee, I do not agree that the federal government or management generally should take unto themselves the right to implement changes without first negotiating them. I ask the minister to give serious consideration to the remarks which have been made in this debate. I say that every individual has the right to free collective bargaining and that no new rule changes should be enforced until the persons concerned have had an opportunity to sit down at the bargaining table and take a look at the proposed changes.
I read in a newspaper that a private mail delivery service is to start in British Columbia and will move east. An editorial in the Globe and Mail for Tuesday, March 4, 1969, states:
I believe that in four or five years it will be inevitable that private enterprise will take over the business of the post.

I should like to ask the minister whether or not it is the intention of the government to turn over our postal service to private enterprise. I think there is every indication that a predominantly United States owned company which has been handling third class mail is moving into British Columbia and also moving east to provide the service which apparently we cannot provide. It is very unfortunate, after having built up the kind of postal service we have across this country, that we should be confronted now with a situation where we must consider a private mail delivery service. Considering the service we have had in the past I know that the public would not like to see this happen. I am sure also that the minister would not like to see it happen. Therefore I believe we should have an explanation in this regard.
I was also bothered by a report I read in a newspaper concerning the committee that dealt with the rate increases. The minister, who was present before the committee, is reported to have said that if publications are valued by their subscribers they will be able to raise their subscription rates. Then he said that though he was sorry to put it so ruthlessly he was prepared to see them cease publication. We are now dealing with the new Department of Communications. I suggest that what the minister said about the increase in postal rates being borne by the people who wish to have the publications is not in keeping with what is sought to be accomplished under this bill.
Dealing directly with the Department of Communications I should like first of all to congratulate the minister on the appointment of those who are to be responsible for planning, operation, regulation and research and development in the new department. I am sure, as he indicated in his speech of February 28, that these people are worthy of our support. I am sure also that every Canadian can be proud that we have people in this country who will devote their time and energy to ensuring that we will have something of which we can be proud in respect of satellite communications. There are a number of questions which come to mind which no doubt the minister will answer when he has an opportunity.
When he introduced his new department the minister indicated that it will be a small one which will reflect the growing importance of communications and the government's increasing involvement in this area, I am sure
March 10, 1969	COMMONS
all of us can appreciate the fact that the respective areas of the department can work very closely, but the prime objective of the department is to establish a national communications policy and program that will tie together all the disparate parts of Canada.
I am sure everyone in Canada would agree that all parts of Canada should be tied together as closely as possible. Of course, if we use the analogy of the postal department we realize what was accomplished there is now being downgraded to the extent that one may wonder whether there is any sincerity in setting up another department and in the same breath suggesting that the disparate parts of Canada are going to be tied very closely together.
Part of the program of the new department will be a review of current telecommunications legislation. The Postmaster General has publicly admitted that our current telecommunications legislation is completely out of date and inadequate to meet changing needs. He stated in the house that not sufficient information is available to the public and especially to his new department from companies such as the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. One of my colleagues will have something to say about the Bell Telephone Company of Canada very shortly.
When we look at the various clauses of this part of the bill we see that the objective of the department is a good one. The idea of a Department of Communications is a good one. However, additional government reorganization is certainly necessary to make the new department really responsible for the growing importance of communications in the country. The present role is a very limited one. For example, most of the responsibility for present communications systems in Canada comes under regulatory agencies such as the Canadian Transport Commission and the Canadian Radio-Television Commission.
Under the satellite program the government commissioned Dr. P. M. McIntosh, general manager of the Bank of Nova Scotia, to submit a report advising the government concerning a plan for the corporate, financial and senior management structure of the domestic satellite communications corporation. Dr. McIntosh has handed down his report, but I understand it has not yet been released. I think it should be recognized that Dr. McIntosh has a background in private industry. I believe his recommendations regarding the new satellite corporation will permit extensive private industrial participation without
DEBATES	6413
Government Organization sufficient public control. When I looked at the white paper issued some time ago it was my belief that there must be sufficient public control. It is up to the minister to ensure that the people of Canada really know what is going to happen in this field.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
If we look at the pros and cons of the establishment at a satellite communication system in Canada we will see they are still quite complex and that there are many conflicting statements by government spokesmen in this regard. It may be useful to have a satellite communication system in Canada, but I personally consider that it is our obligation to see that Canada has control of this system. I am not prepared to agree with the proposal that we make use of the satellite projects of other countries and rent space. I believe we have the wherewithal and the technical knowledge to put a satellite in orbit for use by the entire nation.
We have to ask the minister certain questions and we will have to receive specific answers. We must have a direct comparison of the costs of a satellite system and a terrestrial microwave relay system. This is something we should know about. I realize that the minister said to my colleague, the hon. member for Selkirk, that such a comparison was increasingly difficult to make at this time, but in general the cost of a terrestrial microwave system is proportional to distance whereas satellite system costs are independent of the distance between earth stations. In any event the difference in price is something the minister should be prepared to estimate and inform us about at this time.
Let me return to the social aspect of our communications systems under the new Department of Communications. We realize that the minister indicated before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications that the satellite system would be devoted to Canadian aims and objectives and would be programmed in a way acceptable to the Canadian people, their cultural requirements and needs. I suggest that with the present postal situation this social aspect may be a little hard to sell. Over the weekend I was in an area of central Saskatchewan where the post offices are to be closed on Saturday afternoons. I have drawn this matter to the attention of the Postmaster General, but it seems to me that somewhere along the line we have lost our understanding of the fact that in rural areas the people do get
March 10, 1969

Government Organization together on Saturday afternoons. In central Canada Saturday afternoons perhaps do not mean too much. If you live in the west in some of these small areas you will realize that the people do mix socially on Saturday.
It is true that communication, in addition to that provided by the Post Office, helps to maintain communities such as we have in rural areas of western Canada, and we must have these communities if we are to retain this nation as we know it. I ask the minister to give serious consideration to the need to keep post office wickets open on Saturday afternoons in rural areas. This may seem to be a trivial matter but I assure the minister it is not trivial so far as the rural people are concerned.
It has been stated that a satellite television system would be able to blanket the rural and northern areas of Canada and thus attain greater unification of the country. Let me add to what I have said about communication in this country that it will remain united if the minister will give further consideration to the subject I mentioned previously. I realize that the trend now is for some of the people in rural areas to move to urban centres. Out in the west at this time the trend now is to move back to the rural areas. This was not evident ten years ago. You can travel throughout some rural areas at this time and see new homes, buildings and the like. I believe the social consequences have to be taken into consideration if we are concerned in this House of Commons about communication.
Another point which I think has been rightly referred to in the white paper concerns the limited space we have available in so far as the location of a satellite is concerned. This matter has to be dealt with on an international basis rather than in a hodgepodge way with each country going out as it likes into outer space. I hope the minister is successful in his efforts in this regard. I am sure he will agree that this should be an international arena in which every country would co-operate in respect of space and the location of satellites.
It has been said that with the construction of a satellite system there would be some spin-off benefits to the country involving the development of future markets. We must look very closely at what we are considering in this particular area. It is worthy to note that both of the firms which submitted design programs for the contractors included in their bids participation by foreign firms.
[Mr. Skoberg.3
For example, the bid by Northern Electric, which is a Canadian subsidiary of Bell Telephone, further complicates the question of responsibility and control and includes substantial assistance for Canadair Limited, an American subsidiary of Hughes Aircraft Company of California. The bid by R.C.A. Victor, an American subsidiary, includes additional assistance from Spar Arrow Space Products Limited of Toronto, a systems group of T.R.W. and Company of California. Northern Electric has stated that its proposal will achieve a 64.5 per cent Canadian content under the program. R.C.A. Victor has declared that its proposal will promote the participation of Canadian companies to the maximum degree feasible. In view of these statements I think we should pay particular attention to ensuring maximum participation of Canadian companies in the development of our satellite. The proposals are inadequate for two main reasons, one relating to foreign ownership and the other relating to private development and participation.
Considerable time and money have been spent in this country to determine what foreign ownership is really aE about. We have had in Canada too many experiences in developing private industry expertise. It is only fair to state what I am referring to in this regard. We have had the experience of developing private industry expertise in the Canadian atomic reactor program under Canadian General Electric while at the same time Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, a public corporation, was involved in similar development.
A recent decision by the United States parent of Canadian General Electric has forced the cancellation of the atomic reactor program. Of course, the implications with regard to R.C.A. Victor and its development of a Canadian satellite system are especially important. It is worthy of note that aU patents developed in Canada by Canadian R.C.A. are taken out only by the United States parent. I am sure the minister realizes the situation but I want to draw it to his attention. We should really look at the situation to see whether there is specific justification for government departments and agencies, such as the research and development branch of the minister's department and Crown agencies such as the National Research Council, Atomic Energy of Canada, and the Defence Research Board, to be involved in the construction of a Canadian sateUite.
March 10, 1969

I am a great believer in the idea that we should use the facilities and the people we do have for development in this particular area, particularly for the Canadian satellite. I urge the minister to ensure that these various boards, committees and research councils will be used to their utmost in complete correlation on various programs. I ask the minister to pay particular attention to this.
Some of the research programs we have had in the past have actually been cancelled. This is why I believe there should be some question raised here as to what real development there has been and what exploratory talks have been carried out in respect of a communications satellite. Why have some of our other programs been cancelled in the past? Why was the intense neutron generator program cancelled last fall? Why has the government expended its oceanographic research program under the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources? Why was the Queen Elizabeth telescope project in British Columbia cancelled after millions of dollars had been spent? It was completely wiped out by the stroke of a pen. I think the minister should explain these moves very thoroughly when he answers the questions put to him.
Which department is responsible for industrial research and development programs? Once again we are getting into a situation where we have to ensure that there is complete responsibility in a particular department. We have seen too many varied programs being carried out without parliament knowing whether a department has complete authority in a specific area. I suggest that the minister give us some answer in respect of this particular phase. It is in this area that government scientific research is quite literally chaotic. I say this with all sincerity because, as the secretary of the Treasury Board said some time ago, the national science policy is determined by accident. I am sure that no one in the house would like to see a new department set up that would determine policy by accident.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I again urge the minister to realize that in the communications field the Post Office and the satellite communications system about which we are talking will have to work together to be of the utmost benefit to the people of this country. It is fine to say that we are going to cover the north to the south and the east to the west with a satellite communications system, it is
Government Organization fine to say that we will have tracking stations and the wherewithal with which to provide television coverage and all the other types of coverage necessary for an effective communications system, but we must not allow our main method of communications to deteriorate.
I refer, of course, to the postal service. In his speech of February 28 the minister referred to bulletin boards in post offices and said that while communication unites people it can also isolate them. I agree completely. The minister then said:
It was in this context that I recently threw out the idea of using our nation-wide complex of post offices as locations for communication centres, perhaps by bulletin boards, perhaps by a system of hot-line telephones by which individual members of the public could communicate directly with their government.
I hope that the few post offices left in the rural communities will not have bulletin boards installed where an attempt will be made to post bulletins from hot-line telephones and our new communications satellite. The people in the country using post offices now want to see the written word and are not prepared to see inaugurated a system which would mean they could communicate only by picking up a hot-line telephone. I am sure we are many years away from such a system. I am also certain we are still in the era where we must have an efficient postal service. I subscribe to the new department; I subscribe to the new communications system and commend the minister for the appointments he has made in this field. I wish him well in this area. But unless he changes his tune in so far as the Post Office Department is concerned, I am sure he will not have the support of the house for the new department.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, part II of this bill affords hon. members an opportunity to discuss what some of us consider to be a matter of urgent public importance. My colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough, very clearly and succinctly outlined in his remarks today on his motion to adjourn the house under Standing Order 26 why it is a matter of urgent public importance. It is one of urgent public importance because what is happening poses a serious threat to a vital public service in this country, that of the delivery of the mails.
In my view this threat stems from the minister's intransigence and stubbornness in handling this matter. Because of the minister's attitude and the stand he has taken the Post Office Department, which has afforded
March 10, 1969

Government Organization good service in this country for the last 100 years, is in turmoil. It is in turmoil because we have a Postmaster General who does not seem to understand the fundamentals of good labour relations. The minister cannot say that he was not warned about this situation. The hon. member for Hillsborough, hon. members of the N.D.P. and other members of the opposition have raised this matter day after day in the house. Indeed, on February 28 the Council of Postal Unions issued a press release which was circulated to all members of the house, again warning the minister. I will read briefly from that press release which is over the signatures of the co-chairmen of the Letter Carriers Union of Canada:
The Postmaster General has made public statements that morale is high in the Post Office. He insinuates that there is good dialogue between the union and management. He states at times we are in agreement. However, on the most important issue regarding the new system of delivery he fails to inform the public that the situation is explosive.
That warning from the postal unions came on February 28. It might be worth while if I continued quoting from this release:
Mail service in the meantime is deteriorating. Inefficiency is fast becoming the new guide to operation.
I quote another part of the press release:
We have no objection to a five-day delivery week. Our dispute is with management's interpretation of the collective agreement. The action we have directed our members to take is in our opinion, and in the opinion of our legal counsel, in accordance with the contract.
It is obvious that a crisis situation has developed in this very important and essential public service. We have already experienced the drastic consequences of one strike in the Post Office and we know the suffering it imposed on the Canadian people. We are now perhaps on the threshold of another strike because of the minister's stubbornness in dealing with this matter, because of his refusal, I submit, to consult his colleague the Minister of Labour who has had such success in these matters. I can only assume that he has not consulted the Minister of Labour because I cannot for the life of me believe that the Minister of Labour would have consented to the provocative and threatening statements made by the Postmaster General, which are causing a threat to the mail service of our country and have already caused a most serious crisis in this very essential service.
Instead of trying to cool the situation, in stead of trying to talk calmly to the people 
involved, the minister takes to the public press and threatens the unions. I ask the Minister of Labour, how successful would he be if he adopted this, attitude? How successful would he have been in settling some of the very serious threats to public services which he has successfully handled if he had resorted to threats of prosecution in the public press? The Minister of Labour knows that this is not the way to settle labour disputes. He knows this is not the way to bring the parties together in order to reach agreement.
If there is a curtailment in this essential service, if the service does cease, we can blame only the Postmaster General for the attitude he has taken throughout; the consequences will rest on his shoulders. I am sure the minister realizes the consequences of a disruption in the mail service. The old age pensioner suffers, the disabled suffer and our veterans suffer because they do not receive their pension cheques. The average working man and woman of this country suffer because they lose a service which is essential to the running of the country, a service which I submit has been carried out effectively and efficiently for the past 100 years.
Perhaps the reason for the difficulties in the Post Office today stems from the fact that we have a Postmaster General who has his head in the clouds. He seems to be more concerned with satellites than with mail delivery.

speechtext:
And, as my colleague interjected, with NATO and trying to do the job which the Minister of National Defence is being paid by the Canadian people to do. I suggest to the Postmaster General that he leave NATO to the Minister of National Defence and that he pay more attention to the essential postal services before he gets too far in the clouds with satellites and communications. As I say, the consequences of a disruption in the postal services are serious because they inflict a hardship on the Canadian people, on old age pensioners, on our war veterans, on those receiving disability pensions, and on the working men and women of this country.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
There are problems in the Post Office which would not provoke the type of statement that the Letter Carriers Union was obliged to make on February 28. There are areas in this country where the postal service has not been improved in the past 50 years. In my own
March 10, 1969

city of St. John's which has more than doubled in population in the last 20 years, we still have the same postal services to serve a population of 100,000 that we had to serve 50,000. These are some of the serious problems with which the minister could come to grips instead of issuing threats to the unions. He should be consulting with his colleague, the Minister of Labour, and he should in fact be sitting down at the negotiating table and taking some tips from his colleague to try to smooth out the situation because this is the only way it can be done.
The minister referred to calling on a third party to deal with the dispute. I hope he will elaborate on this point and let us know exactly who the third party will be who will participate in this regard.
This matter is so serious that we feel obliged to bring it to the attention of the house. We believe that the postal services are essential to the people of Canada, and if there is a disruption in the services I submit it will be because of the intransigence and the provocation of the Postmaster General.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have great respect for the Postmaster General who was my predecessor as president of the Montreal Stock Exchange and did an excellent job there.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: He should have stayed there.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
He has many admirable abilities, one of which, however, is not the ability to handle labour relations. This is no fault of his because, like the previous minister of labour, Mr. Nicholson, the Postmaster General has had no training in the ranks of labour. Rather he has been trained in the classroom and the boardroom, and if one is brought up with that type of thinking one is not in a position to understand the needs and aspirations of labour, the way labouring men think and the things to which they aspire. A man who has not been brought up in the labour movement does not know how to do the most important thing in labour negotiations, that is, to sit down with the workers concerned on an equal and friendly basis and be considered by them as a friend and not as somebody who comes from another stratum of society. He should be able to be trusted by the working man because he has always been on the same side of the fence. I say to the minister that in my view he is not in a position through no fault of his own to handle the present labour negotiations.
Government Organization
In the past few years we have had good ministers of labour such as my former colleague, the Hon. Michael Starr, and the present labour minister. Why have they been good labour ministers? Because they came up through the labour ranks, they understand labour's point of view, they know how to talk to working men, and they are trusted by them. In the early days they were in the rank and file of labour. That is why Michael Starr was a successful labour minister, and the same is true of the present Minister of Labour who is doing a good job. I am glad to be able to say this about him.
I say that in order to work out differences like the present one in the Post Office we must have somebody who has the confidence of postal workers, who can sit down and talk to them as an equal and talk to them in their own language. I believe that if the Postmaster General continues to conduct these negotiations in the present manner because of his lack of knowledge of any other approach through no fault of his own, which I can only describe as a bull in a china shop approach, we are going to have a very serious and lengthy strike of the postal workers of this country.
I urge the minister to take action in the interests of bringing to a close what I believe is a serious labour dispute that will have grave effects on the country for a long time in the future if it is not brought to a sensible conclusion as soon as possible. I urge him to hand over these difficult negotiations with the postal workers to the Minister of Labour who, I believe, has the ability to bring this matter to a quick and sensible solution which will be fair, equitable and satisfactory to both the government and the postal workers. In this way our postal communications can continue in a regular, satisfactory and uninterrupted manner.
