NORTHWESTERN SASKATCHEWAN-SUGGESTED ROAD, RAIL AND BROADCASTING EXTENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity of speaking on the motion proposed by the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu). Commenting briefly first about the suggestion that a highway or road should be built from La Loche to the Lake Athabasca area, I would like to confirm the statement that this route has been pioneered on a winter basis by businessmen of the Meadow Lake area. They have proven that the route is feasible. My understanding is that this pioneering began during the time of the previous Conservative government, which for some reason chose to develop the much more expensive and roundabout route that has been partly constructed some distance east of the route proposed by the hon. member. It is perhaps not too late to correct the mistake made some years ago. In fact, I have been told that the Saskatchewan government is seriously considering making a start on this road north of Meadow Lake. I would hope that the federal government would agree to share in the planning and costs of this project.
I also believe that the proposition that a rail line be built to connect Frenchman Butte, Saskatchewan, with Heinsburg, Alberta, is worthy of serious consideration. The hon. member for Meadow Lake is also pleading for
March 10, 1969

adequate T.V. service to the remote communities of this district. The Postmaster General <Mr. Kierans) is planning a communications satellite which I am confident will make it practical to extend T.V. service to all areas of Canada. In fact, this is one of the main purposes and benefits of this imaginative project.
Some derogatory comments were made in the house this afternoon with regard to the Postmaster General's concern about the satellite program. I am sure the people of these areas who cannot share in some of the amenities enjoyed in the more populous areas of this country are very interested in the early operation of the communications satellite so they may feel that they are equal partners in this Canadian nation.
In further commenting on the motion of the hon. member for Meadow Lake I would like to emphasize that the present government recognizes the urgent need to take a comprehensive look at the problems and potential of various regions of Canada and, in close cooperation with the provincial governments, to assist the people in these regions to develop their resources and raise their incomes to levels comparable with those of other Canadians. It is for this reason that the government is forming a new Department of Regional Economic Expansion to be responsible for regional development. This new department will provide the organization at the federal level necessary to the mounting of a coordinated effort to solve the problems of the underdeveloped regions and areas of Canada.
In the case of northwestern Saskatchewan it has been recognized for some time that the economic returns to people in this area have generally been poor. There has been some agricultural development as far north as Green Lake but this has been characterized as a marginal production area because of a combination of low fertility and poorly constructed soils, adverse climatic conditions, high development costs and limited credit. The lumbering and fishing industries, although significant to a few people, have generally been ineffective in providing substantial levels of income to the majority of the people.
Many different types of programs have already been undertaken to assist in the social and economic development of the area. While much remains to be done, I think it might be useful to comment briefly on some of the activities now under way. For the purposes of my comments I will be referring to the Meadow Lake district, local improvement
DEBATES	6421
Northwestern Saskatchewan Economic Changes
districts 974, 980, 983, 986 and 989, and the area along the line from Green Lake to La Loche. These districts are in the southern portion of the general area described in the hon. member's motion.
The soil resources of this area are rated poor to good from an agricultural production point of view. Early settlement in the area tended to locate in lighter soil areas which more recently have proved unsuitable for cereal production. There is now, therefore, some removal to uses such as pasture and forestry. Crop records show a return of approximately 18 bushels per acre, but this yield should show a gradual improvement as lower quality land is removed from cereal production and better quality land is brought into production.
In an effort to utilize such better quality land, the province of Saskatchewan, with federal assistance under the Agricultural and Rural Development Act, implemented a few years ago an incentive program which made grants of $3.50 per acre available for land clearing. From 1966 to the present time, 216 farmers have cleared a total of 7,023 acres of land for agricultural production in local improvement districts 980, 983 and 989.
Some good quality soil is located in low lying wet areas and some effort is being made in small areas to help farmers protect their lands from periodic flooding. One example of this is in the Rollo Park area where works have been constructed with ARDA support to assist some 60 farmers and to protect 9,700 acres of land. This land is primarily used for fodder production which, along with blueberry pasture, forms a substantial base for livestock production in the area.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
As I mentioned earlier, some low productivity land is being removed from cereal production and is primarily being used for forage production. Under the ARDA program some 9,600 acres of farm land has been combined with 31,400 acres of Crown land for pasture development. Seven pastures have been organized or expanded and 20,860 acres have been seeded to grass, with a potential carrying capacity for 10,450 head of cattle. In addition to these pastures, two hay production projects have been established utilizing 1,440 acres of farm land and 3,380 acres of Crown land on which some 6,400 tons of hay can be produced annually.
The area which I have been discussing, however, is only a small part of a large problem area. To illustrate the magnitude of the
6422	COMMONS
Northwestern Saskatchewan Economic Changes
problem I might use the example of the alternative land use program, also supported by ARDA, in the area south of Meadow Lake stretching to the North Saskatchewan River and, in the east, to the Prince Albert National Park. Twenty pastures have been developed in the area utilizing 81,942 acres of Crown land and 36,980 acres of farm land purchased because it had low cereal production capability. The pastures have been fenced; 51,769 acres have been developed and seeded to grass and it is expected that some 22,690 head of cattle can be grazed each year.
I might also mention that the farm people are attempting to make their lives somewhat more pleasant in the Meadow Lake area. Some 117 farm homes have been provided with water under the Saskatchewan family farm improvement branch program which provides technical service, materials at cost and incentive grants under the farmstead water and sewage program. This has also been an ARDA supported program.
As I have indicated, however, the use of land for agriculture is limited; the full dimension will be more clearly identified when the Canada land inventory maps of soil capability for agriculture are completed and published. The same can be said for forestry, recreation and wildlife development in the area, although it is recognized that there is a tremendous potential for these enterprises because of the vast forests and numerous rivers and lakes in the area. Until the capacity is clearly identified, it is difficult to discuss or to plan the type of communication system most suitable, particularly the road system. However, new roads are being developed and resources development is progressing, particularly in the field of recreation. This development is taking place in accessible areas and in areas where the demand for facilities is increasing for the tourist and hunter.
ARDA has participated in the cost of developing facilities for camp grounds and picnic sites in such places as Meadow Lake Provincial Park, Kimball Lake, Pierce Lake, Greig Lake, Jumbo Lake, Makwa Lake, Chitek Lake, Loon Lake, Green Lake, Canoe Lake, Brightsand, Dore Lake, Little Birch, Ile-a-la-Crosse, La Plonge, Little Amyot Lake, McKay Point, La Loche and Little Peter Pond.
To attempt to plan a program of development for the social and economic betterment of the people in the area of Green Lake and north is a complex undertaking. The potential for development in the traditional use of the

DEBATES	March 10, 1969
natural and renewable resources is somewhat limited and knowledge of these resources is inadequate. The Canada land inventory will be of some help but further specific study is required.
It is known, however, that the capability of the people of the area to take on new activities is in need of development. They have limited experience in work other than hunting, fishing and some lumbering, and the educational level is, generally speaking, quite low among the adult population. An attempt is being made to stimulate and assist people to acquire academic skill and vocational training. Some of the agencies involved in this effort are the Saskatchewan Department of Education, Saskatchewan Department of Natural Resources, Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture, Canada Department of Manpower and Immigration, and the Department of Forestry and Rural Development, the name of which is to be changed.
During the winter of 1968-69 four courses under the occupational training for adults program have been scheduled for Meadow Lake, with a capacity of a total of 144 students. The Saskatchewan department of education is sponsoring six courses of educational upgrading for Canoe Narrows, Meadow Lake, Loon Lake and Big River, with a capacity of 100 students. Under the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons program, nine courses with a capacity of 135 students have been scheduled for Green Lake, Beauval, Buffalo Narrows, Ile-a-la-Crosse, La Loche, Pinehouse and Uranium City.
One particular project under way in the area which is of particular interest is a study of the feasibility of growing wild rice, which could provide a new economic opportunity for people of Indian ancestry in the north. In 1962 a project was designed to do research into the characteristics and growth habits of wild rice in northern Saskatchewan. Interest had been stimulated by the fact that wild rice was growing at Limestone Lake, Potato Lake and Nemeiben Lake, presumably from 1935 plantings, that there was a good demand for the product, that the product was returning significant economic returns to people in Manitoba, Wisconsin and Minnesota, and that wild rice was a muskrat and duck feed and indirectly could affect incomes by stimulating increased muskrat and waterfowl populations. I know a good deal about this in principle, because it is the sort of thing that brought me to this house. In 1956, at a convention of this party which selected the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) as leader of this party, I remember that we discussed very extensively the question of northern development and the road to resources program. At that time I was successful in moving from the floor an amendment. Our party is one which allows a degree of change at its conventions. In respect of the road to resources program, since I came from a district which had for 35 years been promised the type of rail expansion which is referred to in the proposal of the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu), I moved an amendment which was adopted and ultimately became the subject of discussion in this house. One of the first suggestions made in 1958 dealt with the question of the extension of services into the
March 10, 1969

northern part of Alberta and the territories. I am glad to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) here. I give him full marks. During his tenure of office as a minister of the Crown with a responsibility in respect of the north, he was very interested and went up there on many occasions. I believe he should be paid a tribute. Consequently, when I see an hon. member such as the hon. member for Meadow Lake pleading his case before the house I cannot help but concur with him. There is a problem in this country. The hon. member for Meadow Lake and other hon. members have touched on it.
We are now seeing a movement in the central part of this country at an unprecedented scale. We have always had this movement before, but it has been aggravated by the growth of the large metropolitan areas. We had a debate the other day in respect of housing. Housing, sanitation, water and air pollution are all matters which affect the large metropolitan districts. This trend towards urbanization is creating great difficulty for us. I am not suggesting that we should reverse the trend and empty the large cities by sending people up into the northern areas; but I do think we should look at the problem from a long range viewpoint. Across the Pacific from our west coast lie the people of China, Indonesia, Korea, Viet Nam and Japan who inside of 35 years will number four billion. We cannot long continue to hold our northern areas as trustees-and that is all we are; we are trustees primarily for the people of Canada but ultimately for the people of the world-unless we settle them.
When we speak of settling and occupying these areas, we must think of such things as transportation and so on which have been spoken of by the hon. member for Meadow Lake. The north does not just begin at the 60th parallel of north latitude. It commences at various points in different provinces. In the province of Saskatchewan, as in the province of Alberta, one might say that it commences about the 53rd or 54th parallel. The boundaries of our country between the Northwest Territories and the remainder of Canada were laid down by man when he moved about the north, They are neither natural nor economic boundaries. Consequently, it is essential that the federal government participate in programs of this kind.
I shall not recount the various steps in respect of the triumph with regard to the Pine Point railway. It might mention that, because of the calibre of the government and its program of northern development, despite the objection of the then members of the opposi-

tion who talked scathingly about building roads from igloo to igloo, I put forward an amendment and the program at Pine Point became a reality. As a result, hundreds of millions of dollars of new wealth have been created and the gross national product has been increased. The people in northern Alberta and the Northwest Territories have been able to participate in a shining, new development. This is precisely what my good friend the hon. member for Meadow Lake is suggesting. He is suggesting that the present government should consider programs of fiscal and financial incentives; the provision of credit; the construction of railways; the construction of highways and the provision of television and other facilities so that the people would really feel a part of the society in which they live.
Through these means, we could obtain for areas such as northern Saskatchewan, northern Alberta and the Northwest Territories, the population which we must have if we are to hold these areas against the demands of the people in other parts of the world. Although the topography and geography is a little different in Russia-we have the benefit of several large rivers where natural development is taking place-Russia has cities of 500,000 or a million people lying far north of the 60th parallel. Mr. Chairman, part II of Bill C-173 deals with the new Department of Communications. The New Democratic party member for Moose Jaw has dealt with the bill in general. This evening I want to deal with the bill in particular as it applies to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. Subsequent to the application by Bell Telephone Company of Canada, I asked the minister whether the federal government would take a position opposing the application for an increase in the level of its earnings and for a 10 per cent increase in telephone rates. His answer in general was this: he expressed concern with regard to this particular company, indicated that he is reviewing telecommunications legislation and that much of our existing legislation is out of date or inadequate to meet changing needs. In addition, the minister indicated that not sufficient information is available to the public, especially in his new department, from communications companies such as Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
Bell Telephone Company has made application to the Canadian Transport Commission to raise its permissible level of earnings from 6.6 per cent to 8 per cent and for authority to increase basic telephone rates by approximately 10 per cent. It is rather significant that not since 1926, under the Ontario Conservative government of Howard Ferguson, has any government intervened on behalf of telephone users against Bell's periodic applications for rate increases. As a result, Bell's increases have either been granted or, at best, temporarily postponed.
Government Organization
In the absence of any competition, public utility monopolies have traditionally been subject to the regulation of the Board of Transport Commissioners, now reconstituted as the Canadian Transport Commission. It is the function of this body to protect telephone users against exorbitant profits which might be extracted because of Bell's monopoly position. But unlike comparable American regulatory bodies, which vigorously dig out the facts regarding the financial position of public utilities, the Canadian body has played a passive role of merely assessing the information which is submitted to it in its hearings. The result has been a most uneven contest, with organizations like the Canadian Association of Mayors and Reeves passing the hat to collect a few tens of thousands of dollars from their already strapped budgets to try to counter the hundreds of thousands of dollars which Bell is ready and able to spend in presenting its case.
It is very much like trying to kill an elephant with a fly-swatter. In short, the Canadian regulatory body has been little more than a sleeping watch-dog. Unless and until some powerful and influential agency such as the federal government is willing to act on behalf of the people in the hearings before the Canadian Transport Commission, protection of the consumers' interests will go by default. It should be acknowledged that following the reconstitution of the old Board of Transport Commissioners into the new Canadian Transport Commission, the Canadian Transport Commission was empowered to dig out the facts in the manner traditionally followed by American regulatory bodies. But so far the Canadian Transport Commission has given no convincing proof that it is going to operate in an active, rather than the traditionally passive, role. All the more reason, therefore, why the government of Canada must play a part to make certain that the interests of users of telephones are protected. This is why I look to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to protect the interests of telephone users and to present briefs to the C.T.C. for the protection of consumers in this field.
In assessing the validity of Bell's request for a rate increase, the public should bear in mind certain features of this corporation's operations over the past decade. Bell stresses that it has not had an increase in its basic rates over the past ten years. It should be noted, however, that in 1958 its permissible level of earnings was fixed at $2.43 per share,
March 10, 1969

Government Organization or the equivalent of 5.9 per cent on over-all capital earnings. In every year following that board ruling, Bell exceeded the permissible level of earnings, and the federal regulatory body did nothing about it. Throughout the period of 1958 to the mid-1960's, Bell's excess profits, extracted illegally in violation of the board's ruling, amounted to some $37 million. Since this amount remained after paying approximately 50 per cent corporation tax, it simply means that Bell illegally extracted some $75 million from telephone users during that period. In 1964, the situation was reviewed by the federal board. But strange as it may seem, hearings were not focussed on Bell's excess profits over the years but rather on Bell's request to have its permissible level of profits raised so as to legalize its excess earnings.
Even stranger, when the board finally ruled in 1966, it raised Bell's permissible level of earnings to a maximum of 6.6 per cent which, by coincidence, simply legalized the profit levels current at that time. But Bell's defiance of the regulatory authority of the C.T.C. persisted. In its first full year of earnings after the 1966 ruling, its profit levels were in the range of 6.7 per cent or 6.8 per cent. At that point the C.T.C. stirred itself and asked Bell what proposals for rate decreases it had, in view of its excess earnings. In 1968 the return on capital of Bell Telephone's operations amounted to 6.9 per cent. Bell argued that because of the sharp rise in interest rates and construction costs, their excess profits were justified. Patsy-like, the C.T.C. accepted this explanation and agreed to tolerate profit levels in excess of the maximum which they had fixed a year earlier. With that encouragement, Bell is now back asking for a new permissive level of earnings at 8 per cent and rate increases to bring profits up to that level. When Bell argues that for the past ten years it has absorbed rising costs within the same basic rate structure and therefore is now entitled to increased rates, there is an important fact which should be noted. Bell is now reaping unprecedented profits from its expansion over the past years combined with technological progress. The over-all result in the company's financial position was revealed during the hearings of 1964-65.

I wish to seize the opportunity provided by this debate on Bill C-173 to discuss certain problems with respect to the current operations of the Post Office Department. I began this particular discussion last


fall when the Postmaster General's reorganization bill was before the house. At that time, I made a point that what was happening to the Post Office Department represented the reversal of a policy which had been recognized in Canada for the past one hundred years. We have since had an opportunity to discuss this subject in a parliamentary committee but we have made no impact whatever on the minister. I notice that the reorganization bill, in the clause dealing with communications, merely endorses some of the features to which we have been calling attention, inasmuch as clause 12 repeals the Post Office Act, and clause 3 states there shall be a department of the Government of Canada called the Post Office Department over which the Postmaster General shall preside. Clause 3(2) says the minister responsible for communications is to be the Postmaster General, so I would think the remarks I intend to make tonight are quite in order.
I say that the government and the Postmaster General have reversed a policy which is as old as Canada itself. It has always been fundamental and vital to the development of a sense of nationhood in Canada for the government to support communications media of all kinds. There is no need for me to go into a lengthy recital of the manner in which this policy has been carried out over the years. Instead, I shall refer to each of the areas in which support has been given by the government, generously in many instances, for the sake of Canadian nationhood and also for the sake of assisting in the achievement of that very elusive quality in Canada, national unity.
It has become a cliche to say it is almost a miracle that Canada was ever brought together from sea to sea. I do not think it was so much by a miracle as by good, practical common sense on the part of the Fathers of Confederation and those who have since followed in their footsteps. These people recognized that communications is the cement of national unity in this country.
The Government of Canada supported the construction of transcontinental railways. The trans-Canada highway system has been- heavily subsidized, as has the national broadcasting system, first radio and then television, in the interest of national unity. By way of an aside, Mr. Chairman, I think there is good reason to question how valuable the huge subsidies to broadcasting have been in achieving national unity. The current subsidy is about $160 million and it would be possible

to argue that at the present stage of the development and utilization of the mass media we have not yet struck a formula which contributes to a sense of nationhood and national unity in this country.
The Postmaster General, as minister responsible for communications, talks in exultant and enthusiastic terms about the huge sums of money which will be invested in the next few years in the development of a satellite communication system. This is all very necessary in achieving national unity, but in the face of all the evidence we have heard, in the face of all the statements which have been made in this house, the minister, with all the stubbornness of his Irish nature, refuses to accept the viewpoints and the arguments presented by many members on this side of the house.
In his administration of the post office, as we are endeavouring to point out, he is turning back the clock one hundred years because he is insisting that this basic means of communication by the printed word and the written word has to be placed on a foundation of financial solvency. This, I suggest, represents the reversal of a long established policy not only in Canada but in all democratic countries, and constitutes rank discrimination against one type of communication important in rural areas of Canada and favours, particularly sections of Canada where urban areas predominate. For example, one could refer to the Golden Triangle along the St. Lawrence, including Toronto, Hamilton and Montreal. I do not have to repeat these arguments because they have been placed before the minister on the occasions to which I have already referred.

Mr. Chairman, the question of communications is very broad, embracing almost every element of which we have knowledge. It is said, for instance, that while two countries of our earth can almost communicate with other planets, 40 per cent of our world's population cannot communicate with each other, being illiterate. The rest of us who are literate also have trouble in communicating. We have a good deal of trouble in making ourselves understood. For example, examine what goes on in this house, Mr. Chairman.
My intervention in this discussion will be confined-because the question is most immediately urgent-to the old tried and, until recently, true method of communication, the postal service. I speak as a member of this house, and as a member of the N.D.P. who is proud of the record of the post office of Canada as a public enterprise. It has handled billions of pieces of mail a year almost without error and, until a short time ago, with speed and efficiency. I also speak as a former employee of the post office. I was a mail carrier and learned something about the business of mail delivery.
During the last eight or nine years, six or seven different men have occupied the position of Postmaster General. In fact, I have lost count of how many ministers in that portfolio we have had. Last fall the minister announced a program of postal reform for
March 10, 1963

Government Organization Canada. In some respects my party thought it a commendable program which was long overdue. In other respects we felt that suggestions would not be amiss. I put forward some suggestions when I spoke in the house on October 21, 1968, as reported at page 1614 of Hansard for that date. I said, in part:
-we wish the proposed post office legislation referred to a standing committee of this house for detailed study and report.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I also said:
-we welcome the move to increase the second class rates on publications published for a profit as being generally in the right direction, but here again we wish a committee study to be made to ensure that the proposed rate increases are sufficient and are borne by those by whom they should be and do not fall upon publications which are not published for commercial profit but rather for the service of some particular educational, health or co-operative association or union.
Generally speaking, Mr. Chairman, I still believe that was a wise course for us to advance, and it might have been a wiser course for the government to accept.
We in the New Democratic party, and the C.C.F. before us, urged for years and years that the business mail, that the ordinary first class consumer mail pay its own way, but even with the increased rates the business mail of Canada is not paying its own way. Very briefly, I would like to put the following points forward: In relation to today's lamentable situation involving strikes and rumours of strikes in the postal service of Canada, which I feel has come about partly as a result of the lack of communication between the minister and the Post Office operation, the minister at this late hour has come forward with the announcement that the disputed work condition issue is being referred to a third party for a second look. If, as is now said by the minister, the issue is of such substance as to warrant it being looked at impartially by a third party, surely there should be no implementation of the disputed points which have now been referred to others for judgment until the second look has been taken. To do otherwise is to suggest that the second look is automatically going to be in favour of one of the parties involved, in this case the government. To that extent, it will prejudge the issue in the minds of a good many of the postal workers. I think I am right in suggesting to the minister that this will create a further lack of faith on the part of postal employees, just at a time when a greater

degree of communication and confidence is very much to be desired.
I am sure there are members on both sides of the house who would like to see the minister doing what others have also suggested, namely, let us have an all-party pause in the attacks on the postal system and on the minister while the third party, of whom, he has spoken, takes this second look at the immediate question of working conditions in the post office. Until this third party reports, let us also have a pause in the implementation of the disputed conditions.
It seems to me that in the last few months the government has attempted a very strange thing. The government, and in particular this minister, have sought to perform, after many years of delay on the part of both the old parties, what amounts to three simultaneous surgical operations, a risky effort for all concerned.
The postal service of Canada, once one of the finest in the world in one of the most affluent countries in the world, has been diluted, reduced, impaired and cut from a six-day a week to a five-day a week delivery, and I think unnecessarily so. At the same time the price to the ordinary consumer, the first class letter writer and bill payer has had to shoulder a 20 per cent increase in letter rate. Certainly, the business people such as the hydro, the oil companies, the phone companies and so on will pass on their part of the new impost to the consumer.
Now, beyond this, the government finds itself involved with the postal service employees in another dispute, employees whose efficiency and service over many years of substandard working and wage conditions have been a subject of comment in Canada. Here, I think I speak fairly and honestly as a former member of that group. I have already suggested a way of dealing with this particular situation involving the postal employees.
If I may add one more expression of concern at the conduct of the minister and the government in this area it is that hundreds of newspapers, co-operative papers, farm papers, union papers, church papers, association papers and scientific papers, certainly none of them profit making publications, are being faced with such an immense increase in postal rates as to make a number of them cease publication. Perhaps more will have to stop publication in the future. In some cases these rate increases amount to 2,000 per cent.

I wonder should the farmers of Canada, through their associations such as the Farmers' Union and the Federation of Agriculture, which from time to time are critical of the Department of Agriculture, and of the Minister of Agriculture, and rightly so, ask for a subsidy from the Department of Agriculture? Mr. Chairman, I think most of us regret that the department which is closest to Canadians in their day-to-day life should also be the subject of most controversy in Canada today. The difficulties in the Post Office far outweigh those in any other department of government; and believe you me, with this government that takes some doing. Yet this is precisely the state in the Post Office Department at the present time.
I ask the minister this question: Did he have any warning that his difficulties were going to be compounded at this time or did they come like a bolt from the blue? I suggest that the Postmaster General had ample warning.. I suggest that the difficulties of the previous postmaster general gave him a warning. But in addition there has been the Montpetit report, that fat volume put out by the commission outlining the grievances found by that judge of the Quebec Superior Court. He

Government Organization felt those grievances should be remedied. Some of them have been remedied.
In addition, there was the new, collective bargaining legislation which we in this house passed in good faith a few years ago. Combining the factors of Montpetit and collective bargaining, the result was that people who had been content to put up with certain conditions over a long period of time were suddenly faced with the fact that they had a responsibility to themselves to do something to better their conditions, I think everybody in the house will agree with that philosophy. I know I preached it myself when I addressed dinners of postal unions at that time. I said: If you have these working conditions of which you complain, do not sit around and take them any more; get out and take them up with your management. Deal at arm's length with each other, and do your best to remedy them.
That spirit is now abroad in the Post Office of Canada. The Postmaster General takes time out with amateurish dabblings in another minister's department, telling us how NATO should or should not operate. Then, he turns to the Post Office and delivers his offhand pronunciamento. No wonder half the country has postal difficulties. I say those warnings were there before the Postmaster General was elected and, subsequently last fall, became a member of the ministry. He has nobody to blame but himself for what is happening in Canada at the present time.
The minister should have had warning from the events of last year when the increases were brought about which have caused consternation. The difficulties, which still have not been fully assessed in the newspaper field, are very much with us in the magazine field. For example, the March, 1969, issue of the Legion contains an article headed "We Face a Crisis". It was written by the dominion president, Mr. Robert Kohaly, who is also chairman of the national magazine executive committee.i The Legion publication had enjoyed its second class mailing rates for more than 40 years. It was aware that increases were coming. This editorial says:
The Legion had prepared for the increase in second-class rates, roughly from half-a-cent a copy to two cents a copy, and had adjusted its 1969 budget to meet a monthly increase in mailing costs of from $1,300 to $5,000.

-the cost of mailing (the Legion magazine) after April 1 will be seven cents a copy or a monthly mailing expenditure of more than $19,000 or $228,000 a year!

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take part in this part of the debate, and I would not think of letting the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour take me off on that particular track. The part of the bill that interests me concerns the post office. I am one of those who has had some experience over the years watching the operations of the post office, and I have always felt that the Postmaster General of Canada did not have much to do. However, looking back over those years, I can say now that the post office was run very well.
In my area, and I think the same is true in others, people are writing me daily telling me that the postal service has gone back 40 years. We do not live far from Toronto, which is our major business centre. Previously we were able to put mail on the train at night that would be in business offices in Toronto the following morning. Letters mailed from business offices in Toronto were distributed to every community in my area the next morning, usually by ten or eleven o'clock. If this mail missed the five o'clock collection out of Toronto it was delivered in the afternoon. This includes deliveries to the rural routes. maintopic: POWER-URANIUM CITY-ELECTRICAL, SERVICE SUPPLIED BY UTILITY COMPANY
POWER-URANIUM CITY-ELECTRICAL, SERVICE SUPPLIED BY UTILITY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was prompted to raise a question the other day by requests I received from Uranium City and Eldorado, mostly from Uranium City. The question was:
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
-in view of the widespread dissatisfaction with the high cost and poor quality of the service offered residents of Uranium City by the private utility company presently supplying electricity to the area, can the Acting Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources say whether Eldorado Nuclear Limited, the Crown corporation primarily concerned with the development of the community, has considered taking over this service directly, itself, or alternatively, using its considerable local influence to get the service improved?
I have raised this matter, Mr. Speaker, because I received a petition signed by 386 persons in Uranium City, together with a copy of Northland News in which the situation is set out. The petition reads:
We, the people of Uranium City, strongly protest the high cost of our electrical power.
We do not understand why Northland Utilities has not revised and lowered power costs long ago.
We are very much aware of electrical appliance damage and lamp burnouts caused by the utility's wide voltage swings.
We are also apprehensive over the fact that the utility does not provide some form of stand-by plant as protection against line failure, such a failure in 40 below temperatures could result in catastrophe for our families, apart from damage to our homes and property.
Our opinion is that Northland Utilities power rates are ridiculously high,

I was under the impression that the power lines were installed by a Crown corporation some time ago. Eldorado Nuclear Limited is the Crown corporation in question. How a privately owned company known 'as Northland Utility can be allowed to make a mark up of almost 100 per cent at the expense of people living in the area, escapes me. We know that those people are living far from large centres in a mining area. All the same, they cannot see why their electric power rates should be so high. Northland News of
March 10, 1969

January 23, 1969, had this to say, in part, about the matter:
Northland Utilities came under fire Monday night when Town Council questioned power officials about low voltage complaints, customer servicing, the inability to contact company officials based here, and the high cost of power to the consumers.
As I say, this is a mining town, and its people cannot see the need for the very high power rates. I think my remarks have pretty well covered the case. I have a copy of the petition, and I could give it to the minister, together with any pertinent material I have in my possession.

speakeroldname: Hon. Olio E. Lang (Acting Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
maintopic: POWER-URANIUM CITY-ELECTRICAL, SERVICE SUPPLIED BY UTILITY COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Eldorado Nuclear Limited has not considered taking over the services directly, itself. So far as the rates are concerned, these have been under consideration for some time and representations have been made by Eldorado Nuclear Limited. It is hoped that there will be a reduction of rates. Since there have been no direct representations to Eldorado Nuclear Limited about the quality of service, Eldorado Nuclear Limited has not considered using its influence with a view to having the service improved.

Mr. Speaker, some days ago at a winter conference sponsored by the Canadian Institute on Public Affairs and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the chairman of the Science Council, Dr. Solandt, made a speech in which he repeated statements which he had made on other occasions to the effect that improvements are needed in the federal government's science policy machinery, and advising the appointment of a minister for science policy.
On March 5, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if the government was considering making such an appointment and I was told by the Prime Minister that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) was in fact that minister. On another occasion when asked a similar question by my colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent), the Prime Minister pointed to the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang), the hon. member from Saskatoon-Humboldt, as being that minister. On a third occasion when asked the same question he referred to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) as the minister responsible for science policy.
Proceedings on adjournment Motion
This is an extremely important matter, Mr. Speaker. The Secretary of the Treasury Board, Mr. Reiseman, testifying before the Senate committee which is investigating science policy said that the decisions of the government with regard to science policy were largely accidental. When one recognizes the fact that in the last several years government commitments to proceed with three very important scientific research programs have been scuttled, so far as one can see without very serious discussions with the scientific community, one realizes the importance of having a government minister responsible for making decisions in this field.
The Queen Elizabeth Observatory, which was to be built in British Columbia, has been cancelled. The HARP project being conducted by the physics department at McGill University has been scuttled and is now operating out of the United States with scientists in charge who were formerly on the staff of McGill University. Tne ING project which was being pushed very hard by the physicists of Canada has also been scuttled.
I am not an expert on science policy, and I suppose no member of this house is an expert on it. I hold no particular brief for these projects. I am not an expert on them any more than I am expert about the money we spend on medical research, or on agricultural research, or on defence research,-most of which seems to have been a failure-but I would like to think that with respect to the hundreds of millions of dollars that we spend the people and the government of Canada are getting some solid advice from the people who know best. Yet, Mr. Speaker, that does not seem to be the case.
An article which appeared in Science Forum in November 1968, written by Dr. Martin W. Johns, a physicist at McMaster University, said in part:
What science policy there may be seems to be directed by persons who neither understand the legitimate goals of science nor have direct communication with scientists-within or without the government service.
Similarly, Dr. L. E. Howlett, writing in Science Forum in the October 1968 issue said:
Too often the argument in favour of a costly project with heavy continuing commitments is that it is good science and excites the imagination. Too rarely is there a good case to support its direct relevance to Canada's future needs and a realistic appraisal of its probable value to the country as compared with the same money spent on other projects.
Dr. Howlett is a former National Research Council scientist. I could go on. Professor
March 10, 1969

Proceedings on adjournment Motion N. H. Lithwick, writing in the Journal of Canadian Studies in August of 1968, in an article entitled "Science policy in Canada" says the following about our so-called science policy:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
After an examination of the conduct and financing of such activity by government in Canada, it is safe to conclude that there is no science policy, except perhaps the conviction that science is a good thing. This in turn stems from an absence of social policy as a whole, so that scientists have been free to develop their art as it pleases them.
Later, he says:
Indeed, the government has clearly chosen to leave future decisions on science policy in the hands of the scientists.
He concludes his article by saying:
How these priorities will be allocated by a body made up largely of scientists in the absence of a set of articulated public objectives raises our most fundamental fears-fears not at all alleviated by reassurances of the chairman that the Council will co-operate wih social and behavioural scientists.
The point I am trying to make simply is that in my opinion it is the duty and responsibility of the government of Canada to establish a system of priorities so that the money which the government decides Canada can afford to spend in the field of scientific research shall be spent to the best advantage of the people of Canada as a whole. That, in my opinion, requires a minister responsible for science policy who can make reasonably sound decisions in respect of what this country needs after consultation with the scientific community in the government, in the science council, in the universities and in industry, on the one hand and the members of the cabinet on the other hand who know the total needs and commitments of the Canadian people. I submit that despite our science secretariat or council the government does not have such a policy.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-EFFECT OF RATE CHANGES IN NON-PROFIT PUBLICATIONS
POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-EFFECT OF RATE CHANGES IN NON-PROFIT PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like a number of other members of the house I have tried at one time or another on orders of the day and at other times to raise a question concerning the inordinate increase in postal rates on what I term non-profit publications in Canada. I do so again tonight, particularly following what I thought was a rather curious reply made to me by the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) last week when I asked a question of that nature. If I understood him correctly he said at that time that instead of the non-profit publications seeking to have redress through a lower rate of postage, their associations might consider applying to a department of government for some type of subsidy. Therefore, I take this opportunity to raise the question again tonight.
If I understood the minister correctly, his suggestion was that there might be a subsidy for non-profit publications such as scientific reviews, church papers, trade union papers and so on which in some cases have been put out of business or curtailed in respect of their publication because' of the new heavy increases in rates. I think what I should like to do, in backing up my question, is to quote from the position my party expressed last October, as recorded at page 1614 of Hansard:
*-we wish a committee study to be made to ensure that the proposed rate increases are sufficient and are borne by those by whom they should be and do not fall upon publications which are not published for commercial profit but rather for the service of some particular educational, health or co-operative association or union.
Had something like that been done at the time, we would not be in the situation many of us feel we are in today in respect of the curtailment of these publications which are not able, from other financial resources, to meet their costs of publication. I refer to those publications I have mentioned before relating to unions, churches, scientific associations and other such small publications. In my view what the government is doing is actually curtailing communications in these fields.
I am one of those who favour proper and heavy increases in the rates on business publications, and business mail generally. They have been subsidized for many years by the ordinary consumers in Canada who have paid the first class rate. However, this is a very different situation to that which we find described in the Ottawa Citizen which made a
March 10, 1969	COMMONS
review of non-profit publications six or seven weeks ago. On January 29, the Ottawa Citizen in an article had this to say:
Among the hardest hit are the independent Canadian union papers which have lost second class mailing privileges and have been assured by a Post Office official that they have no chance of regaining them. Here are some samples of the postal cost increases these papers face, as of April 1:
From $1,057 per annum to $29,696 per annum- From $9,024 to $84,756-
From $18,000 to $72,000-
This list goes on. I feel that this situation was outlined by another one of these nonprofit publication's put out by the Association of Canadian Welfare Councils. I urge the minister to take a second look at the situation. The Canadian Welfare Council says:
If Canada were to suddenly be without such regular periodicals as Canadian Geographic, Community Planning Review, Canadian Consumer, The Canadian Author and Bookman, The Observer, The Canadian Nurse, and a host of other journals published by professional, ethnic or cultural groups across the country, it would be as though half the lights in a house had suddenly been put out.
As one who has long urged and complimented the minister on his energy and common sense in increasing rates in respect of private mail, I urge him again to take another look at what is happening. Perhaps he will then reconsider the application of such legislation to non-profit papers in Canada. This was perhaps less than well thought out legislation. I hope he will take a second look, just *as he has announced today he is doing in respect of the postal workers' conditions. He should have an impartial second look at this situation.

Mr. Speaker, we have dealt with this question extensively during the debate on postal rates and the postal bill itself. We have attempted to answer the questions as fairly and as objectively as possible during various question periods in the last four or five months. I

[DOT] (10:20 o.m.)
We are faced with a situation in which we are handling 17 newspaper or journal publications for 1J cents. There is no possible way in which the government could recover other than the smallest fraction of its costs in this regard. When a non-profit organization sets itself up in business, it expects to pay the people who work for it. It expects to pay for its paper, ink, printing, legal fees, auditing fees and all the other costs that go into the operations. Why should it not expect to pay the postage rate? Why should it expect to get stamps free or at a cut rate? The exaggeration that has gone on in this area is virtually impossible to believe. For example, a great deal of to-do has been made about the fantastic increases faced by the Queen's Quarterly, a journal that many of us agree is a definite asset to the quality of Canadian life. It is said that publication cannot bear the increases. Subscribers to the Queen's Quarterly will have to pay exactly four cents more a year.
I have dealt with the non-profit publications and editors of the unions and have been able to point out that in most cases, for example, the United Automobile Workers, the increase in postal rates would mean an increased charge to their members of 35 cents a year. A farm and country newspaper, which is indicative and a real example of all the farm newspapers, which has a nominal subscription rate of $1.50 but which in effect charges 98 per cent of its subscribers only 25 cents a year, will now have to charge 35 cents a year.
